excerpts: A combo box helps users select an item from a large list of options.
**More than 15 options.** Use a combo box when there are more than 15 choices in a drop-down list. With so many options, users may find it difficult to navigate with scrolling only.
**Limited space.** Use a combo box for presenting options when screen real estate is limited.
**Limited choices.** When the number of options is small, you can continue to use a `select` or `radio` element.

**Use option strings familiar to users.** The combo box filters by matching strings. Include option text that includes familiar strings or spellings (for example, if using the combobox with a state list, include the postal abbreviation in the option text: District of Columbia (DC)).
**Avoid dependent options.** Avoid making options in one select menu change based on the input to another. Users often don’t understand how choosing an item in one impacts another

**Always use a label.** Make sure your select element has a label. Don’t replace it with the default menu option (for example, removing the “State” label and just having the menu read “Select a state” by default).

This article is about how to apply directional changes in inline or other plain text situations, such as _within_ the `title` element or a `title` attribute, or how to apply a direction to attribute text which is different from that of the surrounding element, and so on. What this article does and doesn't cover You will still need to use markup to establish the default direction for a document as a whole (eg. in the `html` tag), and to change direction for block container elements. Because control codes don't cross paragraph (read as block element ) boundaries, and because control codes cannot manage inheritance and scoping through the markup hierarchy, they are only appropriate for inline use. For example, although a `title` element in the header of an HTML page cannot contain markup, it is still possible to set a default base direction on the `title` element tag (or for it to inherit the direction set on the `html` tag). This article is about how to apply directional changes in inline or other plain text situations, such as _within_ the `title` element or a `title` attribute, or how to apply a direction to attribute text which is different from that of the surrounding element, and so on. It also applies to plain text formats such as WebVTT and CSV.

Tightly wrapping opposite-direction phrases In some cases the bidi algorithm copes fine with bidirectional text, and in others it needs some help. In [Inline markup and bidirectional text in HTML](https://www.w3.org/International/articles/inline-bidi-markup/) we make the case that the easiest approach to marking up bidirectional text is to put markup at the start and end of each directional change in the text. This doesn't do any harm, it avoids the likelihood of missing a situation where markup is needed, and it makes the life of the content author much simpler. You should wrap the relevant text [tightly](https://www.w3.org/International/articles/inline-bidi-markup/) . Similarly, when dealing with Unicode control characters it makes sense to put directional formatting characters at the start and end of each directional change in the text. However, it's important to bear in mind that ranges need to be nested appropriately.
Related issues In this section we illustrate some additional spillover problems that can be solved using directional formatting characters.

If you want to change the direction for a run of inline text you need to indicate a start and end point. For this you need to use one of the following characters to indicate the start of the embedded direction change. |Character |Name |Code point |Equivalent markup |Notes | |LRI |LEFT-TO-RIGHT ISOLATE |U+2066 |dir="ltr" |sets direction to LTR and isolates the embedded content from the surrounding text | |RLI |RIGHT-TO-LEFT ISOLATE |U+2067 |dir="rtl" |ditto, but for RTL | |FSI |FIRST-STRONG ISOLATE |U+2068 |dir="auto" |isolates the content and sets the direction according to the first strongly typed directional character | |LRE |

These characters are invisible, although in some editors it may be possible to show symbols that represent them. You could also use character escapes to represent them, such as `&;` , but in bidirectional source text you may find that the characters in the escape don't stay together. (See [Working with source code markup and code examples for RTL scripts](https://www.w3.org/International/questions/qa-bidi-source.en.html) for more on this.) When you apply directional formatting characters to indicate the boundaries of a directional run, you really want to avoid what's inside the boundaries interacting with what's outside – ie. you want to _isolate_ it. For this reason, in an ideal world you would want to follow the [recommendation](https://www.unicode.org/reports/tr9/) of the Unicode Standard to use RLI and LRI, and avoid using RLE and LRE.

It is interpreting the first two Arabic words and the comma and space as a single directional run in Arabic. **More than 15 options.** Use a combo box when there are more than 15 choices in a drop-down list. With so many options, users may find it difficult to navigate with scrolling only.
**Limited space.** Use a combo box for presenting options when screen real estate is limited.
**Limited choices.** When the number of options is small, you can continue to use a `select` or `radio` element.

**Use option strings familiar to users.** The combo box filters by matching strings. Include option text that includes familiar strings or spellings (for example, if using the combobox with a state list, include the postal abbreviation in the option text: District of Columbia (DC)).
**Avoid dependent options.** Avoid making options in one select menu change based on the input to another. Users often don’t understand how choosing an item in one impacts another

**Always use a label.** Make sure your select element has a label. Don’t replace it with the default menu option (for example, removing the “State” label and just having the menu read “Select a state” by default).

This article is about how to apply directional changes in inline or other plain text situations, such as _within_ the `title` element or a `title` attribute, or how to apply a direction to attribute text which is different from that of the surrounding element, and so on. It also applies to plain text formats such as WebVTT and CSV.

Changing the direction of an inline range of text If you want to change the direction for a run of inline text you need to indicate a start and end point. For this you need to use one of the following characters to indicate the start of the embedded direction change.

What this article does and doesn't cover You will still need to use markup to establish the default direction for a document as a whole (eg. in the `html` tag), and to change direction for block container elements. Because control codes don't cross paragraph (read as block element ) boundaries, and because control codes cannot manage inheritance and scoping through the markup hierarchy, they are only appropriate for inline use. For example, although a `title` element in the header of an HTML page cannot contain markup, it is still possible to set a default base direction on the `title` element tag (or for it to inherit the direction set on the `html` tag). This article is about how to apply directional changes in inline or other plain text situations, such as _within_ the `title` element or a `title` attribute, or how to apply a direction to attribute text which is different from that of the surrounding element, and so on. It also applies to plain text formats such as WebVTT and CSV.

Tightly wrapping opposite-direction phrases In some cases the bidi algorithm copes fine with bidirectional text, and in others it needs some help. In [Inline markup and bidirectional text in HTML](https://www.w3.org/International/articles/inline-bidi-markup/) we make the case that the easiest approach to marking up bidirectional text is to put markup at the start and end of each directional change in the text. This doesn't do any harm, it avoids the likelihood of missing a situation where markup is needed, and it makes the life of the content author much simpler. You should wrap the relevant text [tightly](https://www.w3.org/International/articles/inline-bidi-markup/) . Similarly, when dealing with Unicode control characters it makes sense to put directional formatting characters at the start and end of each directional change in the text. However, it's important to bear in mind that ranges need to be nested appropriately.
Related issues In this section we illustrate some additional spillover problems that can be solved using directional formatting characters.

If you want to change the direction for a run of inline text you need to indicate a start and end point. For this you need to use one of the following characters to indicate the start of the embedded direction change. |Character |Name |Code point |Equivalent markup |Notes | |LRI |LEFT-TO-RIGHT ISOLATE |U+2066 |dir="ltr" |sets direction to LTR and isolates the embedded content from the surrounding text | |RLI |RIGHT-TO-LEFT ISOLATE |U+2067 |dir="rtl" |ditto, but for RTL | |FSI |FIRST-STRONG ISOLATE |U+2068 |dir="auto" |isolates the content and sets the direction according to the first strongly typed directional character | |LRE |

These characters are invisible, although in some editors it may be possible to show symbols that represent them. You could also use character escapes to represent them, such as `&;` , but in bidirectional source text you may find that the characters in the escape don't stay together. (See [Working with source code markup and code examples for RTL scripts](https://www.w3.org/International/questions/qa-bidi-source.en.html) for more on this.) When you apply directional formatting characters to indicate the boundaries of a directional run, you really want to avoid what's inside the boundaries interacting with what's outside – ie. you want to _isolate_ it. For this reason, in an ideal world you would want to follow the [recommendation](https://www.unicode.org/reports/tr9/) of the Unicode Standard to use RLI and LRI, and avoid using RLE and LRE.

excerpts: `unicode-bidi` CSS property Baseline Widely available This feature is well established and works across many devices and browser versions. It’s been available across browsers since July 2015. Learn more See full compatibility The **`unicode-bidi`** CSS property, together with the `direction` property, determines how bidirectional text in a document is handled. For example, if a block of content contains both left-to-right and right-to-left text, the user-agent uses a complex Unicode algorithm to decide how to display the text. The `unicode-bidi` property overrides this algorithm and allows the developer to control the text embedding.
In this article Try it Syntax Formal definition Formal syntax Examples Specifications Browser compatibility See also

Syntax css ``` /* Keyword values */ unicode-bidi: normal; unicode-bidi: embed; unicode-bidi: isolate; unicode-bidi: bidi-override; unicode-bidi: isolate-override; unicode-bidi: plaintext; /* Global values */ unicode-bidi: inherit; unicode-bidi: initial; unicode-bidi: revert; unicode-bidi: revert-layer; unicode-bidi: unset; ``` Values `normal` The element does not offer an additional level of embedding with respect to the bidirectional algorithm. For inline elements, implicit reordering works across element boundaries. `embed` If the element is inline, this value opens an additional level of embedding with respect to the bidirectional algorithm. The direction of this embedding level is given by the `direction` property. `bidi-override` For inline elements this creates an override. For block container elements this creates an override for inline-level descendants not within another block container element. This means that inside the element, reordering is strictly in sequence according to the `direction` property; the implicit part of the bidirectional algorithm is ignored. `isolate` This keyword indicates that the element's container directionality should be calculated without considering the content of this element. The element is therefore _isolated_ from its siblings. When applying its bidirectional-resolution algorithm, its container element treats it as one or several `U+FFFC Object Replacement Character` , i.e., like an image. `isolate-override` This keyword applies the isolation behavior of the `isolate` keyword to the surrounding content and the override behavior of the `bidi-override` keyword to the inner content. `plaintext` This keyword makes the elements directionality calculated without considering its parent bidirectional state or the value of the `direction` property. The directionality is calculated using the P2 and P3 rules of the Unicode Bidirectional Algorithm. This value allows the display of data that is already formatted using a tool following the Unicode Bidirectional Algorithm. **Example queries:** Find docs about onboarding new clients. Tasks mentioning the kickoff meeting. Show all open tasks assigned to me. The Assistant returns matching results with a **link to the matching objects** . You can then ask it to pull out specific content or take additional actions from there.
**📌 If the results aren't right, follow up.** Describe what's missing or ask the Assistant to adjust — you don't need to start over.
Using AI Search in Productive AI Search lets you find tasks, projects, docs, and other objects and content within them while using a plain-language description.

content.executive_summary:
- **One-Query Contract**: Clockify documents `task @project` syntax: users enter the task name, then add `@` plus a project or client to narrow the result [executive_summary[0]] [1]. Harvest takes a simpler approach: users type a project or task name in the selection box and press Enter, while the client is represented by the project [executive_summary[1]] [13]. -> Accept one unqualified query across the full client > project > task path, with optional `@` scopes for disambiguation.

- **Layered Matching**: Notion supports quoted exact strings and exposes a Best Matches mode that gives more weight to page titles and recent edits [executive_summary[2]] [15]. Fuzzy search is a different operation based on similarity measured by Levenshtein edit distance [executive_summary[3]] [5]. -> Use token AND matching as the default, phrase matching as a boost or explicit quoted mode, prefixes while typing, and fuzzy matching only as a controlled fallback.

- **Progressive Disclosure**: Clockify offers a compact hierarchy that collapses projects under their client and separately lets users turn on a task filter [executive_summary[0]] [1]. -> During a query, retain only matching branches and their ancestors; expand the path to a matched task, but do not expand unrelated siblings.

- **Two Search Surfaces**: Linear separates workspace Search from its contextual command menu. Search covers issues, projects, and documents [executive_summary[4]] [7], while the command menu exposes applicable actions and remains searchable and keyboard controllable [executive_summary[5]] [8]. -> Use a combobox for choosing an entity and a command palette for actions, navigation, and scope changes.

- **Explainable Ranking**: Notion's documented ranking gives title matches more weight than body content and raises recently edited pages in Best Matches [executive_summary[2]] [15]. Linear also describes result ordering as relevance-oriented with status ordering [executive_summary[4]] [7]. -> Rank an exact task plus its matched project and client above a parent-only hit, but keep parent hits visible as labelled group results.

- **Keyboard Contract**: WAI-ARIA guidance documents Enter to accept the focused option and Escape to close the popup and return focus to the combobox [executive_summary[6]] [3]. USWDS documents Tab as a way to leave without choosing and Space as a selection action in its combo box guidance [executive_summary[7]] [14]. -> Make Arrow navigation, Enter, Escape, Tab, and clear behavior deterministic and identical in every hierarchy state.

- **Ambiguity and Bidi Safety**: A client may have many similarly named descendants, and mixed Arabic and English follows the Unicode bidirectional algorithm [executive_summary[8]] [27]. W3C describes LRI, RLI, and FSI isolation controls and recommends isolation over embedding for inline directional changes [executive_summary[9]] [17]. -> Show the complete breadcrumb, resource type, and stable identifier; isolate mixed-direction labels at render time and never silently select an ambiguous row.

- **Recoverable Empty States**: The cited product pages do not publish a universal no-results algorithm. -> Preserve the query, say which levels were searched, offer clear and broaden-scope actions, and make fuzzy or natural-language recovery visibly secondary rather than silently changing the result set.

The recommended pattern is therefore a searchable, single-select combobox whose records are denormalized with client, project, and task fields, plus a separate command-palette mode. The critical design decision is to search the entire ancestry as one logical record while displaying the result as a breadcrumbed hierarchy.
content.what_clockify_harvest_linear_jira_notion:
The products are useful precedents, but they do not implement one common three-level picker. Their public documentation exposes different slices of the problem, so the safest conclusion is to borrow interaction patterns, not to claim that every product uses the same matcher.

| Product | Documented hierarchy or search surface | Documented query and result behavior | Keyboard or selection evidence | Boundary of the evidence |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Clockify | Client, project, and task hierarchy; compact mode collapses projects under a client [what_clockify_harvest_linear_jira_notion_agencyanalytics_and_productive_io_actually_expose[0]] [1] | Project/client filtering is available without the task filter; an optional task filter supports `task @project` and `@client` narrowing [what_clockify_harvest_linear_jira_notion_agencyanalytics_and_productive_io_actually_expose[0]] [1] | Favorites can appear at the top of the project finder and are user specific [what_clockify_harvest_linear_jira_notion_agencyanalytics_and_productive_io_actually_expose[0]] [1] | The cited help page does not publish a full scoring formula or confirm fuzzy matching. |
| Harvest | All time is tracked to a task assigned to a project for a client [what_clockify_harvest_linear_jira_notion_agencyanalytics_and_productive_io_actually_expose[1]] [25] | Users choose project and task, type either name in the selection box, and press Enter [what_clockify_harvest_linear_jira_notion_agencyanalytics_and_productive_io_actually_expose[2]] [13] | `N` opens time tracking and `Esc` closes the new time-entry window [what_clockify_harvest_linear_jira_notion_agencyanalytics_and_productive_io_actually_expose[2]] [13] | The client is not documented as a separate picker in this flow. |
| Linear | Workspace Search covers issues, projects, and documents [what_clockify_harvest_linear_jira_notion_agencyanalytics_and_productive_io_actually_expose[3]] [7] | `/` opens Search; `O` + `I` targets issue title or identifier; issue results are ordered by relevance and status [what_clockify_harvest_linear_jira_notion_agencyanalytics_and_productive_io_actually_expose[3]] [7] | Issue ID + Enter opens an issue and Esc clears the search [what_clockify_harvest_linear_jira_notion_agencyanalytics_and_productive_io_actually_expose[3]] [7] | This is a workspace search and issue system, not a client > project > task time-entry picker. |
| Jira | Issue search uses text search and field filters; a Project dropdown broadens the search scope [what_clockify_harvest_linear_jira_notion_agencyanalytics_and_productive_io_actually_expose[4]] [9] | Users can search issues in one project or broaden to multiple projects [what_clockify_harvest_linear_jira_notion_agencyanalytics_and_productive_io_actually_expose[4]] [9] | J and K move between issues; `?` opens the shortcut help [what_clockify_harvest_linear_jira_notion_agencyanalytics_and_productive_io_actually_expose[4]] [9] | The cited page does not document a nested client/project/task selector. |
| Notion | Workspace Search and Enterprise Search cover pages, connected sources, databases, relations, and properties [what_clockify_harvest_linear_jira_notion_agencyanalytics_and_productive_io_actually_expose[5]] [12] | Search opens from the sidebar or Cmd/Ctrl+P or Cmd/Ctrl+K; quotes request an exact string [what_clockify_harvest_linear_jira_notion_agencyanalytics_and_productive_io_actually_expose[6]] [15] | Best Matches weights relevance, recent edits, and titles over body content; filters include Title only, In, teamspace, and date [what_clockify_harvest_linear_jira_notion_agencyanalytics_and_productive_io_actually_expose[6]] [15] | The cited pages do not describe the internal relation-property picker as a three-level tree. |
| AgencyAnalytics | A Client represents one tracked website or URL; dashboards and reports are created within that Client [what_clockify_harvest_linear_jira_notion_agencyanalytics_and_productive_io_actually_expose[7]] [29] | Client management includes list and tile views and checkbox selection in List view [what_clockify_harvest_linear_jira_notion_agencyanalytics_and_productive_io_actually_expose[8]] [30] | No selector-specific keyboard contract is documented in the cited pages. | The cited help pages are client-centric and do not document a nested project/task picker or its matching rules [what_clockify_harvest_linear_jira_notion_agencyanalytics_and_productive_io_actually_expose[7]] [29]. |
| Productive.io | Time on Tasks lets users open a task, use its Time tab, select a Service, and start a timer [what_clockify_harvest_linear_jira_notion_agencyanalytics_and_productive_io_actually_expose[9]] [34] | AI Search finds tasks, projects, docs, and other objects from a plain-language description [what_clockify_harvest_linear_jira_notion_agencyanalytics_and_productive_io_actually_expose[10]] [33] | The cited time-tracking flow does not expose a combined searchable client/project/task picker. | Productive demonstrates a useful natural-language fallback, but its cited help page does not define picker ranking or fuzzy behavior. |

The takeaway is that Clockify is the clearest direct precedent for cross-level time-entry lookup, Harvest is the clearest minimal selection flow, and Linear is the clearest separation between search and actions. Jira and Notion show how scope and field filters can reduce ambiguity, while AgencyAnalytics and Productive.io are important cautionary cases: their public documentation does not establish that a client > project > task picker exists in the same form.

Clockify's decision to make task filtering optional is especially instructive. It supports a compact project/client workflow for people who mostly choose projects, but it also provides an explicit task-oriented mode for people who need task precision [what_clockify_harvest_linear_jira_notion_agencyanalytics_and_productive_io_actually_expose[0]] [1]. That is a better model than forcing every user through an always-expanded three-level tree.

Harvest illustrates the opposite trade-off. Its documented flow is deliberately shallow: project and task are chosen together, and a client is reached through the project relationship [what_clockify_harvest_linear_jira_notion_agencyanalytics_and_productive_io_actually_expose[2]] [13]. This is fast when names are unique, but it places more responsibility on the result row to expose the client context clearly when projects share names.
content.query_semantics_token_and_phrase_boosts_:
The user should not have to know which word belongs to which level. Treat each selectable leaf as a single searchable record with these fields:

`client name + client aliases + project name + project aliases + task name + task aliases + breadcrumb + identifier`

For a query such as `Acme website hero`, the candidate task is eligible when all meaningful terms are found somewhere in that combined path: `Acme` in the client, `website` in the project, and `hero` in the task. This is path-level AND, not field-level AND. Requiring every token to occur in every field would make the common one-query use case fail.

| Matching mode | What it should do | When it should win | What it should not do |
|---|---|---|---|
| Token AND | Split an unquoted query into normalized terms and require every term somewhere in the candidate path | Default mode after two or more characters | Do not require the terms to be in input order or in one level only |
| Phrase | Preserve quoted words as an ordered phrase and boost adjacent, exact matches | Explicit quotes such as `"website redesign"`, or as a ranking boost | Do not make phrase order a hidden hard requirement for ordinary typing |
| Prefix | Match the beginning of a token while the user is still typing | Primary incremental behavior for the last token | Do not let a short prefix swamp exact results from another level |
| Alias and identifier | Match known abbreviations, codes, IDs, and alternate spellings | High-confidence metadata match, especially for repeat users | Do not display an alias without the canonical name and breadcrumb |
| Fuzzy | Permit bounded spelling similarity after exact, token, phrase, and prefix matches are exhausted | Typo recovery, with a visible “Did you mean” or “Fuzzy matches” treatment | Do not silently broaden every token, because false positives are hard to diagnose |

Notion gives a useful precedent for making phrase behavior explicit: its help page tells users to put a search term in quotes when they want an exact word or string [query_semantics_token_and_phrase_boosts_prefixes_and_bounded_fuzzy_recovery[0]] [15]. Its Best Matches behavior also shows why field weighting matters: titles are more likely to rank above page contents, and recently edited pages rank higher [query_semantics_token_and_phrase_boosts_prefixes_and_bounded_fuzzy_recovery[0]] [15]. For a task picker, the equivalent is to weight the task name and breadcrumb more heavily than an arbitrary description or note.

Elastic's definition clarifies why fuzzy search should not be the default. A fuzzy query returns terms similar to the search term as measured by Levenshtein edit distance [query_semantics_token_and_phrase_boosts_prefixes_and_bounded_fuzzy_recovery[1]] [5]. That mechanism is valuable for a typo, but it is not the same as phrase matching, prefix matching, or a deliberate cross-level token match. Mixing all four modes at the same weight makes the result list look arbitrary.

Clockify demonstrates an explicit escape hatch for users who know the hierarchy: enter the task first, then add `@` and a project or client [query_semantics_token_and_phrase_boosts_prefixes_and_bounded_fuzzy_recovery[2]] [1]. The recommended design should support that syntax as an optional accelerator, while keeping ordinary unqualified typing first-class. In practice, `Acme website hero` should work, and `hero @website @Acme` should narrow the same index without changing the underlying result model.
content.tree_behavior_and_ranking_preserve_the_c:
A hierarchy is useful for context, but it is a poor result layout when every node is expanded before the user knows what matches. Search should temporarily create a result tree, not mutate the user's saved tree state.

| Where the query matches | Rows to retain | Expansion behavior | Ranking behavior |
|---|---|---|---|
| Client only | Matching client plus a count of matching or available projects | Keep projects collapsed initially; expand on Arrow Right, click, or an explicit “show projects” action | Show as a client result, not as an arbitrary task result |
| Project only | Client ancestor and matching project | Expand the client and project path; keep unrelated projects hidden | Rank above a client-only hit when the picker target can be a project |
| Task only | Client, project, and task ancestors | Expand exactly the matched path and show the task row highlighted | Rank highest when the field expects a task, because the leaf is the actionable match |
| Parent and descendant | The complete matched path and any directly relevant sibling needed for context | Expand the path; do not open every sibling | Give the leaf match priority, retain the parent as a labelled group or separate selectable result |
| No match | No stale tree rows | Keep the popup open with recovery actions | Do not substitute recent or favorite items without labelling them as suggestions |

The core rule is ancestor preservation. If a task matches, the client and project must remain visible so two identical task names can be distinguished. If only the client matches, the interface should not pretend that every descendant matches; it should show the client as the hit and let the user expand it deliberately.

Clockify's compact list is a concrete example of the space problem. It collapses all projects under the client and offers a wider expansion for long project or client names [tree_behavior_and_ranking_preserve_the_client_project_task_path_without_expanding_the_world[0]] [1]. Its optional task filter also separates project/client lookup from task-heavy lookup [tree_behavior_and_ranking_preserve_the_client_project_task_path_without_expanding_the_world[0]] [1]. The design lesson is not that Clockify has a documented smart-search expansion algorithm; it is that hierarchy density should be user-controlled and task detail should not be forced into the default view.

Ranking should be explainable. A practical order is: exact full path, exact task with exact parent context, exact project or client plus a strong descendant, prefix match, alias match, and finally fuzzy match. A parent-only result remains visible because it may be the intended selection, but it should not outrank an exact child when the field is asking for a task. The row should show the matched fragment and the complete breadcrumb so the user can see why it ranked where it did.

This approach also handles parent selection safely. If a client or project is not a valid value for the current field, render it as a group header rather than an option. If it is valid, give it a distinct type label and selection action; never make Enter on a parent silently choose its first child.
content.combobox_versus_command_palette_a_two_su:
A nested entity picker and a command palette solve different problems. A combobox answers “which existing client, project, or task should I assign?” A command palette answers “which action or destination should I invoke?” Combining them produces a menu in which a task name, “create project,” and “open settings” compete with no clear selection model.

USWDS recommends a combo box for large lists, using more than 15 options as one example, or where screen space is limited [combobox_versus_command_palette_a_two_surface_interaction_contract[0]] [14]. It also says that a combo box filters by matching option strings and that option text should contain familiar strings or spellings [combobox_versus_command_palette_a_two_surface_interaction_contract[0]] [14]. For a hierarchy, that means the visible option string must include the canonical name plus enough ancestry to disambiguate it, not merely a leaf label.

| Surface | Primary purpose | Input and result model | Enter and dismissal | Recommended use |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Entity combobox | Choose one client, project, or task | Editable text input with a filtered list of typed options and breadcrumb metadata | Enter accepts the focused option; Escape closes and returns focus to the input [combobox_versus_command_palette_a_two_surface_interaction_contract[1]] [3] | Time entry, assignment, relation, filter value |
| Browseable tree popup | Inspect hierarchy before choosing | Tree rows with separate expansion and selection affordances | Arrow Right/Left changes expansion; Enter selects only a valid option | When the user knows the parent but not the leaf |
| Command palette | Invoke actions or navigate | Searchable commands grouped by scope and action type | Enter invokes the command; Escape returns to the invoking control | Create, open, move, assign, change scope |
| Filtered issue/workspace search | Find an object rather than set a field | Search result list with type, status, and metadata | Enter opens the object; scope shortcuts refine the search | Linear- or Jira-like navigation |

Linear is a strong case study for the separation. Its `/` shortcut opens Search across issues, projects, and documents [combobox_versus_command_palette_a_two_surface_interaction_contract[2]] [7], and `O` + `I` gives a more specific issue search by title or identifier [combobox_versus_command_palette_a_two_surface_interaction_contract[2]] [7]. Separately, its command menu exposes actions applicable to the current view or selection and remains searchable and keyboard controllable [combobox_versus_command_palette_a_two_surface_interaction_contract[3]] [8]. The implication is direct: use one visual language for search, but use distinct modes and result types.

The minimum keyboard contract should be stable whether the list is flat or hierarchical. Typing filters without moving focus from the input. Down and Up move the active result. Right expands a collapsed parent and Left collapses it without selecting. Home and End move to the first and last visible result. Enter selects the active valid option. Escape closes the popup and returns focus to the input. Tab leaves without committing. A clear control removes the query without selecting a row.

WAI-ARIA's documented Enter and Escape behavior supports the most important part of this contract [combobox_versus_command_palette_a_two_surface_interaction_contract[1]] [3]. USWDS also documents Tab as an escape from selection and Space as a selection action in its component guidance [combobox_versus_command_palette_a_two_surface_interaction_contract[0]] [14]. Test the implementation with screen readers and keyboard-only use; USWDS explicitly warns that assistive-technology testing has revealed combo-box concerns and recommends considering a select component where appropriate [combobox_versus_command_palette_a_two_surface_interaction_contract[0]] [14].
content.failure_proofing_ambiguous_labels_arabic:
**Ambiguous tokens.** A query such as `strategy` may match a client, several projects, and dozens of tasks. Do not resolve ambiguity by choosing the first lexical match. Show a type badge, full breadcrumb, status, and stable identifier. If two rows remain tied, keep both and make the user choose; an explicit `@project` or `@client` scope, modelled on Clockify's syntax [failure_proofing_ambiguous_labels_arabic_english_bidi_permissions_and_empty_results[0]] [1], is a useful accelerator.

**Parent-only matches.** A client or project match should be visible even when no descendant name matches, but it must be visually and semantically distinct from a task match. A parent hit can be a selectable result only if the field accepts that entity type. Otherwise it is a context row with an expansion affordance. This prevents the dangerous failure mode in which Enter selects a project because its name happened to contain the same token as the intended task.

**Arabic and English in one label.** The rendering layer must not use the visual order of mixed-direction text as the search key. W3C notes that direction metadata is needed for bidirectional text and defines LRI, RLI, and FSI for isolating inline runs [failure_proofing_ambiguous_labels_arabic_english_bidi_permissions_and_empty_results[1]] [17]. Use logical, normalized strings for token matching, then render each label with direction metadata appropriate to its content. Isolate embedded English identifiers, numbers, or Arabic labels so an ID does not visually migrate to the wrong side of a breadcrumb. W3C specifically recommends the isolation approach and says RLI and LRI are preferable to RLE and LRE [failure_proofing_ambiguous_labels_arabic_english_bidi_permissions_and_empty_results[1]] [17].

MDN explains that mixed RTL and LTR display is governed by a complex Unicode algorithm and that `unicode-bidi` and `direction` affect embedding and isolation [failure_proofing_ambiguous_labels_arabic_english_bidi_permissions_and_empty_results[2]] [27]. In practical terms, do not manually reverse strings, reorder tokens for display, or use a visual label as a parsing shortcut. Keep the query text intact, normalize it in a separate search representation, and test Arabic-only, English-only, and mixed labels with IDs, punctuation, and numbers.

**Empty results.** Keep the typed query visible. The first line should say `No matches in Client, Project, or Task`, followed by actions such as `Clear search`, `Remove last token`, `Search all levels`, and, where permissions allow, `Include archived`. Do not replace the user's query with favorites or recent items; if suggestions are shown, label them as suggestions. Notion's explicit source and context controls provide a useful model for scope recovery: users can choose all sources, a specific source, a page, or a teamspace [failure_proofing_ambiguous_labels_arabic_english_bidi_permissions_and_empty_results[3]] [12]. Productive's AI Search demonstrates a separate natural-language route across tasks, projects, docs, and other objects [failure_proofing_ambiguous_labels_arabic_english_bidi_permissions_and_empty_results[4]] [33]. These should be recovery modes, not silent changes to the original picker query.

AgencyAnalytics is a useful boundary case. Its cited documentation defines a Client as one website or URL and places dashboards and reports inside it [failure_proofing_ambiguous_labels_arabic_english_bidi_permissions_and_empty_results[5]] [29], while its client-management documentation shows list and tile management rather than a documented nested task picker [failure_proofing_ambiguous_labels_arabic_english_bidi_permissions_and_empty_results[6]] [30]. That argues for an explicit “scope not supported here” state instead of pretending every product has the same hierarchy. Productive makes the opposite move by offering broad natural-language search, but its task time flow still documents selecting a Service inside a task's Time tab rather than a combined three-level picker [failure_proofing_ambiguous_labels_arabic_english_bidi_permissions_and_empty_results[7]] [34].
content.recommended_product_specification_one_qu:
Implement the picker as a leaf-oriented index with denormalized ancestry. Every result should carry immutable IDs for client, project, and task, canonical display names, aliases, type, active or archived state, permission visibility, and a breadcrumb. Search those fields together, but score and display them separately.

| Specification area | Required behavior | Acceptance test |
|---|---|---|
| Query entry | One text field accepts `Acme website hero`; all tokens may match different levels | A task under client Acme and project Website is returned when Hero is the task name |
| Optional scoping | Support explicit scopes such as `hero @Website @Acme`, while keeping unqualified typing equivalent | Adding a valid scope narrows results without changing the canonical result identity |
| Matching order | Exact token/path first, phrase and prefix boosts next, aliases and bounded fuzzy recovery last | A typo cannot displace an exact result; fuzzy rows are visibly labelled |
| Result row | Show type, matched fragment, and full `Client / Project / Task` breadcrumb | Two identical task names remain distinguishable without opening either record |
| Tree state | Query mode shows matching branches and ancestors only; browse mode restores the normal tree | A task hit expands exactly its path and does not expand unrelated siblings |
| Parent ranking | Child hit outranks parent-only hit when the field expects a task; parent remains visible as context or a typed option | Enter never chooses a parent when the field only accepts tasks |
| Empty state | Preserve input and expose clear, remove-token, broader-scope, and permission/archive recovery actions | No-result recovery takes one keyboard action and does not erase the query |
| Accessibility | Label the input; expose popup state, active option, result type, and selected state; implement deterministic Arrow, Enter, Escape, Tab, and clear behavior | A keyboard-only user can search, expand, choose, cancel, and retry without a pointer |
| Internationalization | Match normalized logical text; render mixed-direction labels with direction metadata and isolation | Arabic, English, numbers, and IDs remain in the intended visual order and remain searchable |

The input should not require users to learn syntax, but the syntax should reward expertise. `Acme website hero` is the default. Quoted phrases such as `"website redesign"` request exact phrase behavior, following Notion's explicit convention [recommended_product_specification_one_query_explainable_results_and_measurable_guardrails[0]] [15]. A task-first form such as `hero @Website` follows Clockify's documented narrowing pattern [recommended_product_specification_one_query_explainable_results_and_measurable_guardrails[1]] [1].

Use a clear ranking explanation when needed: `Matched task: Hero; project: Website; client: Acme`. This is more useful than an opaque relevance score. Linear's documentation describes relevance and status in result ordering [recommended_product_specification_one_query_explainable_results_and_measurable_guardrails[2]] [7], and Notion documents title and recency weighting [recommended_product_specification_one_query_explainable_results_and_measurable_guardrails[0]] [15]; the proposed picker should expose the equivalent information through field-specific highlighting and breadcrumbs rather than claiming that relevance is self-explanatory.

Instrument the experience around outcomes, not just keystrokes. Measure time to first correct selection, first-result acceptance, backtracking, no-result recovery, accidental parent selection, duplicate-label errors, keyboard-only completion, screen-reader completion, and mixed-direction rendering defects. Segment these metrics by hierarchy depth, query length, language direction, and permission scope. A lower keystroke count is not a success if it increases wrong-client selection.
content.synthesis:
The evidence reveals four distinct philosophies. Clockify is **hierarchy-aware and operator-assisted**: it preserves client/project/task structure, offers compact collapse, and gives expert users `task @project` narrowing [synthesis[0]] [1]. Its trade-off is that the user may need to understand task-filter mode. Harvest is **shallow and fast**: project and task are typed into one selection box, while the client is inherited through the project [synthesis[1]] [13]. Its trade-off is less explicit client disambiguation.

Linear is **command- and navigation-oriented**: it searches multiple object types and separates that from contextual actions [synthesis[2]] [7][synthesis[3]] [8]. Jira is **filter-oriented**: text search, field filters, and a project scope solve breadth without presenting a client/task tree [synthesis[4]] [9]. Notion is **field- and scope-oriented**: exact quotes, title-only filters, recency, source controls, and context selection make ranking and scope visible [synthesis[5]] [15][synthesis[6]] [12]. These models optimize different time horizons: immediate assignment, object navigation, structured investigation, or workspace discovery.

AgencyAnalytics is **client-container-oriented**, defining dashboards and reports within a client rather than documenting a comparable three-level picker [synthesis[7]] [29]. Productive is **hybrid and natural-language-oriented**, pairing task-local time tracking with broad AI Search across objects [synthesis[8]] [34][synthesis[9]] [33]. The tension is important: broad natural-language search improves recall, while a transactional picker must optimize precision and prevent accidental selection.

The final design decision should therefore be a hybrid, not a literal copy of any one product: use Clockify's cross-level and explicit-scope ideas, Harvest's low-friction Enter selection, Linear's separation of search from actions, Notion's visible scope and field weighting, Jira's filters, and W3C/APG's focus contract. Make token-level path matching the stable core; make phrase, prefix, and fuzzy behavior progressively more permissive and visibly labelled. Preserve the tree only as context around a ranked leaf result. That combination gives users one natural query while keeping every selection explainable, reversible, and accessible.
